title: The Square-Root Key: a machine for manufacturing primes

lines.text: Come along on a discovery. Prime numbers: two, three, five, seven, eleven. They build every other number, yet nobody has found the pattern in how they arrive.

In 1994 Robert Sacks, out of pure curiosity, sketched the counting numbers on his notepad as a spiral. Let's do the same: break the grid open and let every number find its place. Only the two stays lit, our first prime.

Two times two. Count two dots. The two nearer the centre is the multiplier: it copies the row one level up, the copy slides along the Sacks spiral, and its final dot lands on four. Looking back, nothing landed on three, so three is prime.
Two times three lands on six, so five is prime. Two times four lands on eight, so seven is prime. Three times three, three rows of three, lands on nine.

Every new prime joins the multipliers. On to thirty: eleven, thirteen, seventeen, nineteen, twenty three and twenty nine are never landed on. Whatever no multiplication reaches is a prime. Now let's see what Sacks saw.
This is Sacks's spiral: every number n at a distance of root n from the centre, one full turn per square. Fill it in the way he did, and the primes stop looking random.
lines.footnote: Sacks spiral: n at radius √n, angle 2π√n

lines.text: Bend the Sacks spiral over a saddle. Composites fill the valleys, and whole routes from the centre appear: some with no primes at all, others crowded with them.
In red, the squares, n equals k squared. One lands at the end of every turn, all on one ray, and a square is never prime.
In blue, n equals k times k plus one: a number times its neighbour, always even, never prime. It runs out on the opposite side from the squares.
In green, Euler's route, n equals k squared plus k plus forty one: forty primes in a row, every one of them on this saddle.
Humans carried this search for twenty three centuries, from Euclid to Riemann. In the age of AI discovery, the last lock will be opened by humans and machines together.
Zeno's puzzle: walk half way to the wall, then half of what is left, then half again. The steps shrink so fast that you never pass two.
Now a gentler rule: every step is one over the square root of its number. One, one over root two, one over root three.
Shrinking this slowly, the chain never stops: it runs off the floor forever. Hold on to that square root, exponent one half. It is the key to everything that follows.

chapters.title: The Stage
chapters.subtitle: A floor, a pole, and a dial

lines.text: The chain lives on a floor, the complex plane, with a pole going up. The pole is a dial, and its reading is called t. Turn it, and every joint of the chain begins to bend.

chapters.title: Turn the Dial
chapters.subtitle: The tip keeps finding the centre

lines.text: Two rules. The lengths follow square roots. The bends follow logarithms: each arrow turns away from the leg before it by t times the log of n over n minus one. As the dial climbs, the turns keep winding.
Why logarithms? Riemann, in 1859, let the power of n be a complex number, and a complex power does not stretch. It turns, by the logarithm of n.
lines.footnote: n^(−s) = e^(−s · log n): a complex exponent rotates, and the rotation is proportional to log n

lines.text: The chain is endless, but the arrows we skip wind up like a spring around one centre, and one orange arrow, Euler and Maclaurin's, jumps straight to it.
lines.footnote: orange: Euler–Maclaurin tail N^(1−s)/(s−1) + N^−s/2 + Bernoulli terms

lines.text: Keep turning. The tip wanders, then dives straight into the centre.
At fourteen point one three it hits dead centre: a collision. Stack the first twenty turns end to end: together they wind t times the log of twenty one, almost seven full turns.
Turn on, and the collisions never stop: twenty one, twenty five, thirty. Hardy proved there are infinitely many. These heights are the famous zeros of the Riemann zeta function.
Start with an ordinary cosine wave and a dial, gamma, that sets its speed. Turn the dial up, and the ripples pack tighter.
Put a logarithm inside, and the ripples bunch up near zero. Dial it to fourteen point one three: the first collision's wave.
The second collision is born as its own cosine, winds up, and sinks into the master wave. Where they agree the peaks reinforce; where they disagree they cancel.
Wave after wave, hundreds of them. What survives are sharp spikes on two, three, five, seven, eleven and thirteen, and faint ones on the squares.
A map of the primes, built from nothing but collision heights.
Riemann's recipe turns the collisions into a count of the primes, one piece at a time. Start with the straight line y equals x.
Subtract the logarithm of two pi, a constant shift, and a small correction from the trivial zeros that fades away.
Now the first collision's wave. It grows like root x and oscillates with log x. On its own, it only bends the line.
Add the second and third waves, then hundreds more. The steps sharpen on the primes, with smaller steps on the powers of primes.
With enough collisions the staircase lands on the exact count: a step at every prime, as tall as its logarithm.

chapters.title: The Square-Root Key
chapters.subtitle: Why one half, and nothing else

lines.text: Back to the key: every arrow was one over root n, exponent one half. Change it to zero point nine, and the tip never hits the centre. Watch the miss.
Picture every exponent between zero and one as a strip. Our collisions all sit on the one half line.
Suppose they strayed off that line. Slide the exponent toward zero point nine, and the staircase wobbles off its rails.
lines.footnote: red: the staircase if every collision had exponent β instead of ½

lines.text: The Riemann Hypothesis says it never happens: every collision, forever, on the one half line.
In October 2026, OpenAI published an AI generated proof that no collision can stray past seven eighths, and by symmetry none below one eighth: the quasi Riemann hypothesis.
lines.footnote: openai/math, family 003 · manuscript Sept 30, 2026 · released Oct 6, 2026

lines.text: It is machine checked in Lean, but human peer review is still under way: a strong claim, not settled fact.
lines.footnote: Lean: riemannZeta s ≠ 0 for 7/8 < Re s · independently re-checked · not yet peer reviewed

lines.text: The orange gap, from one half to seven eighths, is where the Riemann Hypothesis still lives.
Back to the Sacks spiral on its saddle. The primes, the most irregular objects in arithmetic, seem to follow a rule written into the numbers themselves.
One last picture, and this one is a guess, not a result. Let the zeta trail rise from the centre of the Sacks spiral, with a collision wherever it returns to the axis.
lines.footnote: a visual hypothesis, not a theorem

lines.text: Each collision's wave is born at its own height, runs out along the Sacks spiral, and sinks onto the saddle, building the master wave.
From above, the master wave spikes at every prime. Dial in all ten thousand collisions, and the spikes sharpen, prime after prime.
Saddle, trail and waves: one structure seen three ways. Prove the one half key, and we will have read one line of the instruction set. The picture is yours now. Explore it.
